body_markdown:
Since production ended in 2002, the Nissan Skyline GT-R R34 has become less a car and more a folk legend. Sadly, these days it’s also more of a financial instrument, and prices now align with those of starter homes. But spending six figures on one of these cars introduces a problem: Can you really use all its capabilities, given that its limits are so high?


There is another R34, however. The rear-wheel-drive Skyline 25GT Turbo, known almost universally as the GT-T, is not merely the R34 for people who cannot afford Godzilla. On the road, it can be more entertaining.


This is not an argument that the GT-T is secretly better at everything. It is not. The GT-R has the stronger RB26DETT engine with its twin turbos, a six-speed Getrag gearbox, ATTESA E-TS four-wheel drive, larger brakes, and swollen bodywork. Launch both from rest and the GT-R disappears while the GT-T negotiates with its rear tires.


Wikimedia Commons/FotoSleuth


But road driving is not a standing-start demonstration, and the numbers are closer than the badges suggest. The GT-T’s 2.5-liter RB25DET NEO straight-six was officially rated at 276 horsepower and 253 lb-ft. Under Japan’s informal 1989 gentleman’s agreement to cap advertised horsepower, the GT-R was also quoted at 276 hp, with 289 lb-ft. A manual GT-T coupe weighs around 3100 pounds, roughly 287 pounds less than a standard GT-R and 330 pounds less than a V-Spec II. Much of that saving comes from losing the GT-R’s four-wheel-drive hardware, but the smaller brakes, five-speed gearbox, narrower wheels, and slimmer body also help.


That’s rather important. Depending on the test, the GT-T reaches 60 mph in 5.5 to 6.0 seconds, against 4.8 seconds for the GT-R. Once rolling, though, it does not feel like the consolation prize. The single turbo wakes around the useful end of the rev counter and the car surges forward with the slightly industrial determination that makes RB engines addictive. It has less outright violence, but you can use more of it without accidentally applying for low-earth orbit.


Even with an extra pair of doors, as in the 25GT-X Turbo above, the R34 family of Skylines are undeniably attractive.


Nissan


The R34 arrived in 1998 as Nissan’s replacement for the R33. It was shorter, tighter, and visually angrier, with a bluff nose, four round rear lights and enough straight edges to furnish a small kitchen. The GT-R arrived the following year and stole the posters, game covers, and film roles. The rest of[the Skyline range](https://www.importavehicle.com/blog/complete-guide-to-nissan-skyline-r34-models-gt-gt-t-gt-r-v-spec-more) did the less glamorous work, offered as coupes and four-door sedans with naturally aspirated or turbocharged straight-sixes.


The GT-T lacks the GT-R’s pumped arches and deep front bumper, but that is part of its appeal. In standard form it sits on 17-inch wheels, which are narrow enough to look almost delicate by modern standards. There is less theater and less temptation to fit a bodykit designed during a migraine. A clean GT-T has the same square-jawed R34 shape, without looking as though it is permanently waiting for its next restraining order.


Broad Arrow


Nissan


The R34 family resemblance is obvious, but where the GT-R (left) bulges with menacing purpose, the GT-T is far more subtle.


Inside, the distinction is equally useful. You do not get the GT-R’s central multifunction display broadcasting boost pressure, temperatures, and front-to-rear torque split like a miniature mission control. Instead, there are three simple gauges angled toward the driver, solid gray plastics, and seats that look ordinary until you realize they hold you properly. It is peak late-1990s Nissan: Everything works, even if it feels like anyone wearing a roll-neck was noticeably absent from the interior design considerations.


The mechanical recipe is gloriously straightforward. The RB25DET NEO uses variable valve timing, a single turbo and a five-speed manual gearbox to drive the rear wheels. Multilink suspension sits at both ends, with Super HICAS rear-wheel steering adding some intrigue. The steering is lighter, the body moves more, and the narrower tires surrender earlier. These are advantages, not defects.


Nissan


Nissan


A GT-R attacks a corner by marshalling systems. You turn in, commit, and feel the car distribute power with unnerving competence. It flatters you, then encourages you to arrive faster next time. The GT-T asks more questions. The front takes a set, the rear follows, and the throttle becomes part of the conversation. In the dry it can be neat and accurate. In the wet it becomes a 276-hp lesson in manners, delivered after the furniture has been moved.


Such adjustability is why the cheaper car can be more fun, more often. You do not need circuit speeds to feel it working. The engine has enough torque to move the chassis around, but not so much that every squeeze of throttle becomes an insurance event. Sure, the five-speed gearbox is less glamorous than the GT-R’s Getrag six-speeder, yet its ratios suit the RB25’s broad delivery, and the shift has the mechanical feel of industrial switchgear.


They’re eligible for import, and they *are* out there, though buying one today is where the celebration meets reality. GT-Ts were cheap for years, but most of those years occurred before we could get them in the U.S. They are visually close enough to a GT-R to attract people with fiberglass catalogs, and many became drift cars, replicas, or rolling exhibitions of abandoned ideas. Factory manual coupes are scarce, automatics are common, and conversions vary enormously in their execution.


Mecum


Mecum


Mecum


Various[Japanese exporters](https://jdm-expo.com/5-nissan) feature them in[their inventory](https://www.jdmbuysell.com/for-sale/nissan/skyline/r34/?srsltid=AU7gw4VRkmURsb4cBoiZ1GSoqMy2aDyXP-XKq7ewfkZFrWN-FK1vV3N0) , and JDM specialty dealers like[Top Rank](https://www.importavehicle.com/inventory) in California and[Japanese Classics](https://www.japaneseclassics.com/inventory/?make=Nissan) in Virginia seem to have a reliable stream of all sorts of R34s coming through their showrooms: Japanese Classics recently sold a 23,000-mile five-speed GT-T for $50K. They are rarer still on the auction circuit; Bring a Trailer offered[a modified car](https://bringatrailer.com/listing/1998-nissan-skyline-gt-t-2/) in 2025, which was a no-sale at $39,500, while Mecum has sold exactly one,[a 42,000-mile car](https://www.mecum.com/lots/1124262/1998-nissan-skyline-r34-gt-t-tommykaira-25r-coupe/) with a Tommykaira 25R body kit (pictured above), for $56K, back in 2024. At one-third the price of a[#2 (excellent) GT-R](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/nissan/skyline/2000/2000-nissan-skyline-gt~r?id=aCn1I000000kJaqSAE&condition=excellent) , some might view it as money very well spent.


Anything being offered by a reputable dealer *should* be car you’d want to own, but buy the shell before the modifications. Check the rear arches, sills, chassis rails, trunk floor, and suspension mounting areas. Confirm the gearbox was born manual—or converted properly. Inspect the cooling system and be suspicious of any heroic power claims unsupported by invoices. An RB25 will tolerate sensible tuning, but nearly three decades of boost controllers and optimistic mapping can test any friendship.


The R34 GT-T will never replace the GT-R in collector mythology, and good. Mythology is expensive, heavy, and increasingly reluctant to leave the garage. The lighter Skyline gives away traction, braking hardware, and ultimate pace, then repays you with movement, accessibility, and rear-wheel-drive mischief. Put aside the badge hierarchy, and you find the R34 that can still be driven as its maker intended.


Godzilla wins the argument. The GT-T wins the afternoon.
